title: Trait Theories (Allport, Cattell, Eysenck)
summary: Trait approaches to personality: Allport's cardinal/central/secondary traits, Cattell's 16 Personality Factors (source and surface traits), and Eysenck's PEN model (Psychoticism, Extraversion, Neuroticism).
objectives: Describe Allport's cardinal, central and secondary traits.
Explain Cattell's 16 source traits and the 16PF.
Describe Eysenck's PEN model and its biological basis.
revision: Trait theories: Allport's cardinal/central/secondary traits; Cattell's 16 source traits (16PF); Eysenck's PEN model (psychoticism, extraversion, neuroticism).
traps: Cattell: 16 source traits via factor analysis (16PF).

notes.t: Dominant traits that shape most of a person's behaviour (rare, e.g., altruism in Mother Teresa).
Core characteristics used to describe a person (e.g., honest, kind, outgoing).
Situation-specific preferences (e.g., food choices, minor likes/dislikes).
Cattell used factor analysis to identify 16 source traits (underlying dimensions) and surface traits (observable clusters). The 16PF questionnaire measures these.
Eysenck linked traits to biological differences (cortical arousal, autonomic reactivity), making his model biologically grounded.
UGC NET frequently contrasts Allport's trait categories with Cattell's 16PF and Eysenck's PEN dimensions.

mnemonics.title: ACE
mnemonics.text: A — Allport (cardinal, central, secondary), C — Cattell (16 source traits, 16PF), E — Eysenck (PEN: psychoticism, extraversion, neuroticism)
